progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From b01: homeostasis, tolerance range and set point; the five parts; thermoreceptors in skin and hypothalamus; the hypothalamus as control centre; shivering and narrowing skin arterioles in the cold; negative feedback opposes a change and fades as it succeeds. From Year 11: neurons carry nerve impulses; hormones travel in the blood to target cells; heat moves from hotter to cooler. Not assumed: endotherm, ectotherm, vasodilation, vasoconstriction, evaporative cooling, thyroxine, countercurrent exchange, the three adaptation types.
progression.startsWith: Connect neural and hormonal signals to effectors. The video opens: In late November twenty eighteen, a heatwave hit far north Queensland, and Cairns reached over forty-two degrees.
progression.stopsAfter: defining an endotherm (most body heat from its own metabolism, used with controlled heat loss to keep core temperature fairly steady) against an ectotherm (most heat from the surroundings, still regulates by behaviour); tracing how thermoreceptors and the hypothalamus send fast nerve impulses to skin arterioles and sweat glands (the neural pathway) and slower hormones in the blood, such as thyroxine raising metabolic rate in a long cold spell (the hormonal pathway); explaining vasodilation (widened arterioles carry more warm blood near the surface, so more heat is lost to cooler air; vessels don't move) and sweating (cooling by evaporation, less effective in humid air); classifying adaptations as physiological (body processes that switch on and off), behavioural (actions) or structural (body features), with the red kangaroo using all three and features that cross categories; naming trends (large heat-shedding extremities in hot climates, compact insulated bodies in cold, countercurrent exchange); explaining why feedback can fail when hot air adds heat, dry heat loss is limited and evaporation needs water that runs short.
progression.nextLesson: test heat loss with a model experiment (route entry bio-m8-p01).

teaching.task: In November 2018, a heatwave in far north Queensland killed about 23,000 spectacled flying foxes in two days, even though flying foxes pant, lick themselves and fan their wings to cool down. How do endotherms usually keep body temperature in range, and why can that fail?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why vasodilation loses heat (more warm blood near a surface, cooler air; 4); why sweat cools (evaporation takes energy; 5) and why humidity defeats it (5); why hormones are slower (they travel in blood; 6); why the kangaroo's licking works (evaporation over a dense vessel network; 8); why countercurrent exchange keeps heat (heat crosses from artery to vein; 9); why feedback failed in 2018 (hotter air adds heat, so the animals relied heavily on evaporation, which needs water; 10). Attention: a real Australian event that poses the question (1) and is answered with the physics just taught (10). Visual medium: a heat-balance beam that tips with each effector, and a matched warm and cold skin pair. Apply: explain and predict (12a), classify and explain on an unseen animal (12c). Remember: "widen and wet, narrow and shiver" and the three questions.
teaching.conversationalApproach: In late November 2018 a heatwave pushed Cairns past 42 degrees and roughly 23,000 spectacled flying foxes died in about two days, even though they pant, lick themselves and fan their wings, so the question is how endotherms regulate body temperature and where that control runs out. Endotherms make most of their body heat from their own metabolism and control heat loss to keep core temperature fairly steady, unlike an ectotherm such as a lizard. When core temperature rises, thermoreceptors in the hypothalamus and the skin detect it and the hypothalamus sends fast nerve impulses to the skin. Arterioles relax and widen (vasodilation), carrying more warm blood near the surface so more heat passes to cooler air, and sweat cools by evaporation, which takes energy from the skin and works far less in humid air. In the cold the loop runs the other way, and thyroxine, a slower hormonal signal, raises the metabolic rate. Adaptations are physiological, behavioural or structural, and the red kangaroo shows all three, while trends across endotherms link ears, limbs, fur, blubber and countercurrent exchange to climate. The flying foxes died because hotter air added heat instead of carrying it away, leaving evaporation using water they were already losing. The memory aid is hot means widen and wet, cold means narrow and shiver. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: In late November twenty eighteen, a heatwave hit far north Queensland, and Cairns reached over forty-two degrees. In about two days, roughly twenty-three thousand spectacled flying foxes died. These animals pant, lick themselves and fan their wings to cool down. So how do animals like them usually keep their temperature in range, and why did it fail here?
teaching.understandingCheck: 12a is an explain and predict item (hypothalamus, two effectors, humidity), matching the marker comment on 2021 Q29 and 2025 Q24 ("the causal path from response to temperature change"). 12c is a classify and explain item on an unseen endotherm, the koala (the stop: compare behavioural, structural and physiological responses). Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the whole card stays on screen during the countdown and after it. Feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): the answer, the key reasons, givens underlined in the card as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B8-IQ1-02 (p 56): "investigate the various mechanisms used by organisms to maintain their internal environment within tolerance limits, including:" with the listed examples "trends and patterns in behavioural, structural and physiological adaptations in endotherms that assist in maintaining homeostasis (ACSBL099, ACSBL114)" (scenes 7 to 9, attempt 2) and "internal coordination systems that allow homeostasis to be maintained, including hormones and neural pathways (ACSBL112, ACSBL113, ACSBL114)" (scenes 3 and 6). The third example, "mechanisms in plants that allow water balance to be maintained (ACSBL115)", belongs to b05. "Within tolerance limits" is carried by scene 10.

design.visualSystem: A heat-balance bar owns the top of the frame from scene 3: a horizontal beam with "heat gained" on the left pan and "heat lost" on the right pan (coded outline, abstract), which tips as effectors switch on and levels when temperature is back in range. Below it, the working area holds one painted plate at a time with its callouts. b01's loop ring appears as a thumbnail at the upper left in scenes 2, 3 and 6, its effector slot lighting to show where the current plate sits in the loop. People are never drawn: skin appears as the matched warm and cold skin cross-section plates; the "body" is never outlined. At most three bright text items at once; earlier labels dim to grey.
